title: while/repeat loops that hit max_iterations report success, silently truncating the run
existing_state: Both loop containers stop at max_iterations (default 10000: Services/Scripting/Commands/WhileCommand.cs:14, RepeatCommand.cs:15) and then return `new CommandResult { Success = true, ... }` after emitting only a Warning-level line (WhileCommand.cs:105-110, RepeatCommand.cs:85-90). The triggering condition is exactly the dangerous one: the `while`/`until` expression is stuck (typo'd variable name evaluating to a constant, a `send`-captured value that never changes, etc.). The script burns up to 10000 iterations of real SSH commands against the host, abandons the loop mid-work, and then continues to the following steps — and the overall run is recorded as successful in history and job results. Nothing sets _last_error, the result is not marked SuppressedError, and `on_error` has no effect since nothing failed.
recommendation: Make hitting the cap a failure by default (CommandResult.ApplyOnError with a clear message, so `on_error: continue` still allows opting out), or add an explicit `on_max_iterations: fail|continue` option on while/repeat with fail as default. At minimum set _last_error and mark the result SuppressedError so post-run checks and notifications can see the truncation.
user_benefit: A stuck loop condition surfaces as a failed step instead of a quietly truncated run that history marks green — critical when the loop is doing real work against production hosts.

evidence.note: cap reached -> Warning emit only, then Success=true returned
identical silent-success pattern in repeat

title: switch silently treats an invalid 'matches' regex as no-match
existing_state: A switch case written as `value: "matches <pattern>"` compiles the pattern at runtime; if the regex is invalid (typo like an unclosed paren, or a variable substituted into the pattern producing bad syntax), the bare `catch { matches = false; }` at Services/Scripting/Commands/SwitchCommand.cs:47-50 swallows the ArgumentException and the case simply never matches — no warning, no error, nothing in the output. Execution falls through to the default branch (or no-op at :83-84), so the script takes the wrong path on every host with zero diagnostics. There is also no parse-time validation of `matches` patterns in ScriptParser, so the mistake survives editing, canvas round-trips, and scheduled runs indefinitely.
recommendation: In the catch block, emit a Warning ("switch case N: invalid regex '<pattern>': <message>") via context.EmitOutput so the misroute is visible, and add a validation-time check in ScriptParser.ValidateSteps that attempts Regex construction for case values starting with 'matches ' and reports a script error before the run starts.
user_benefit: A typo in one regex no longer silently reroutes every host down the default branch — the author finds out at validation time instead of discovering wrong actions were taken fleet-wide.

evidence.note: regex branch: catch { matches = false; } with no emit — invalid pattern is indistinguishable from a legitimate non-match

title: int()/float() return 0 on unparseable input, making 'parse failed' indistinguishable from a genuine zero in threshold logic
existing_state: TypeFunctions.ToInt returns 0 when the input cannot be parsed as a number (Services/Scripting/Functions/TypeFunctions.cs:27-46 — the final `return 0;` at line 45 covers any non-numeric string); ToFloat returns 0.0 the same way (TypeFunctions.cs:48-62). Combined with regex_match returning "" on no-match (StringFunctions.cs:197), a common monitoring pattern like `if: int(regex_match(output, "(\\d+)% used", 1)) > 90` silently evaluates to `0 > 90` = false whenever the device output format shifts — the alert branch simply never fires, on every host, with no signal. Conversely `if: int(x) == 0` fires the zero-branch on garbage input. There is no way for a script to distinguish these cases today.
recommendation: Return null on parse failure instead of 0 (the engine already handles null values distinctly throughout ValueResolver/comparison logic), and/or add an optional second argument `int(x, default)` so scripts can opt into a fallback explicitly. If backward compatibility forbids changing the return, at minimum emit a runtime warning through the step output so multi-host runs show that a conversion failed.
user_benefit: Threshold and health-check scripts are this app's bread and butter; today a format change in device output silently disables alerts fleet-wide. Distinguishing parse failure from zero makes those scripts trustworthy.

evidence.note: ToInt: non-numeric string falls through to `return 0;`
ToFloat: same pattern, returns 0.0
regex_match returns "" on no-match — composes with int() into a silent false condition

title: regex_replace() silently returns the unmodified source on an invalid pattern — sanitization/redaction steps can no-op with zero signal
existing_state: RegexReplace catches both RegexMatchTimeoutException and ArgumentException (invalid pattern) and returns the original source string unchanged (Services/Scripting/Functions/StringFunctions.cs:165-176). A script using regex_replace to strip secrets, ANSI codes, or sensitive fields from device output before logging/notifying — the docs themselves recommend a regex_replace incantation for ANSI stripping — gets the raw, unsanitized text back if the pattern has a typo or a variable-built pattern is malformed, with no error, no warning, nothing in output. regex_match has the related problem that an invalid pattern and a legitimate no-match are both "" (StringFunctions.cs:194-208), so a script cannot tell 'pattern broken' from 'value absent'.
recommendation: Distinguish the two failure modes in StringFunctions: an ArgumentException (user wrote a bad pattern — deterministic, will fail on every host) should fail the step or at minimum set _last_error and emit a warning; a RegexMatchTimeoutException can keep the soft fallback but should still warn. Apply the same treatment to regex_match/regex_match_all/regex_groups, which currently swallow ArgumentException into empty results (StringFunctions.cs:224-225, 248-249).
user_benefit: When a redaction or extraction pattern is broken, the owner finds out immediately instead of discovering unsanitized output in logs/notifications, or extraction silently yielding empty values across an entire fleet run.

evidence.note: catch (ArgumentException) { return source; } — invalid pattern returns input unchanged
regex_match: invalid pattern and no-match both return ""
regex_match_all/regex_groups swallow ArgumentException into empty lists

title: iif() bare catch turns a broken condition into 'always take the then-branch'
existing_state: Iif evaluates its condition with ExpressionEvaluator inside a bare `catch` (Services/Scripting/Functions/MathFunctions.cs:184-193): when evaluation throws — e.g. `iif(lenght(x) > 0, "up", "down")` where the unknown function makes ExpressionParser throw FormatException (ExpressionParser.cs:436) — the fallback re-resolves the ENTIRE condition string as a plain value via JsonUtilities.ResolveJsonValue (MathFunctions.cs:191). That resolution falls through to the literal string "lenght(x) > 0" (per the fall-through at JsonUtilities.cs:312-333), which is non-empty and therefore truthy, so the then-branch is taken unconditionally. Any typo or evaluator error inside an iif condition thus silently pins the result to the true-value on every host, every run.
recommendation: Narrow the fallback in MathFunctions.Iif: only fall back to truthiness when the condition contains no comparison/logical operators (the legitimate 'simple value' case the comment describes); let FormatException from the evaluator propagate so the step fails with 'Unknown function: lenght'. This also becomes moot for the typo case if the unknown-function fall-through (BUG-010) is fixed.
user_benefit: iif is the branching primitive people embed in set:/send: lines; today a typo flips it into a constant. Propagating the parse error makes the failure visible at the exact step instead of producing confidently wrong branch decisions fleet-wide.

evidence.note: bare catch at 188-193 re-resolves the condition as a value; literal string is truthy
the FormatException that gets swallowed
fallback path resolves the condition text to itself as a string

title: Division and modulo by zero silently return 0, propagating bad numbers into downstream decisions
existing_state: In ExpressionParser, `/` and `%` with a zero right-hand side emit a Warning line and substitute `0.0` rather than failing: `if (rhs == 0) { _context.EmitOutput("Warning: Division by zero, returning 0"...); left = 0.0; }` (ExpressionParser.cs:234-243 for `/`, 249-257 for `%`). Since denominators in this tool are frequently derived from command output (e.g. `set: pct = ${used} / ${total} * 100` where a host returns total=0), the expression yields 0 instead of erroring, and that 0 then commonly drives an `if`/threshold (`if pct > 90`) — so a host with no data is silently classified as 0% healthy and the wrong action is taken. The warning is buried in normal output and the step still reports success.
recommendation: Make divide/modulo-by-zero fail the enclosing step (throw a FormatException from ExpressionParser, which ExecuteStepCoreAsync already funnels into CommandResult.ApplyOnError), or at minimum return a sentinel that conditions treat as undefined rather than the false-but-valid value 0. If a silent default is kept for back-compat, gate it behind an explicit script option.
user_benefit: Arithmetic on missing/zero host data fails visibly instead of quietly producing 0 and steering threshold logic into the wrong branch.

evidence.note: div and mod by zero both return 0.0 with only a warning

title: Encoding functions return wrong data instead of failing: hash() silently computes SHA256 for any unknown algorithm; hex_decode() drops the last nibble of odd-length input
existing_state: CreateHashAlgorithm's switch ends with `_ => SHA256.Create()` (Services/Scripting/Functions/EncodingFunctions.cs:104-115), so `hash(data, "crc32")` or `hash(data, "sha3-256")` returns a SHA256 digest with no error — and the intended guard `if (hasher == null) return null;` at EncodingFunctions.cs:67 is dead code because the factory can never return null. Separately, HexDecode sizes its buffer with integer division `value.Length / 2` (EncodingFunctions.cs:86-88), so an odd-length hex string like "abc" decodes only "ab" and silently discards the trailing character instead of rejecting clearly-corrupt input (the existing catch at :91-94 would have returned null had the loop been allowed to hit the bad slice).
recommendation: Change the switch default to return null so the existing null-check at line 67 does its job (hash() then returns null for unknown algorithms, consistent with base64_decode's failure behavior). In HexDecode, return null when value.Length is odd before allocating the buffer. Both are one-line fixes in EncodingFunctions.cs.
user_benefit: Scripts that verify file checksums or decode device-emitted hex get definitively wrong answers today instead of a detectable failure; a checksum comparison against the wrong algorithm fails confusingly, and truncated hex decodes pass through as plausible-looking data.

evidence.note: `_ => SHA256.Create()` — unknown algorithm silently becomes SHA256
dead null-check that the fix would reactivate
value.Length / 2 truncates the final nibble of odd-length input

title: extract silently exports every named regex group as a script variable, clobbering existing variables of the same name
existing_state: On every successful single-match extraction, ExposeNamedGroups (Services/Scripting/Commands/ExtractCommand.cs:195-208, called from ExtractSingleMatch at 124) iterates all named groups in the pattern and calls context.SetVariable(group.Name, value) for each — unconditionally overwriting any existing variable with that name. The only trace is a Debug-level line (206) that is invisible unless debug mode is on. A pattern like `(?<host>\S+)\s+(?<status>\w+)` silently replaces the `host` / `status` variables (including CSV-column-derived variables like a `status` column) for all subsequent steps of the run, with no opt-in and no warning. Note the named group also wins even when the group didn't participate in the match (empty string overwrites the old value).
recommendation: Make named-group export opt-in (e.g. `export_groups: true` on extract, or only export groups not already present), or at minimum emit a Warning-level (not Debug) message when an existing variable is overwritten by a named group. Also skip groups that did not participate in the match (Group.Success == false) so an optional group can't blank an existing variable.
user_benefit: Stops a regex author's incidental group names from silently corrupting unrelated script state (host/credential/loop variables) mid-run — a class of failure that today is nearly undebuggable because the overwrite leaves no visible trace.

evidence.note: every non-numeric group name SetVariable'd unconditionally; only Debug-level output
ExposeNamedGroups invoked on every single-match extract before into-assignment

title: assert substitutes variable text into the condition before parsing — quotes/operators in data break or alter the expression (diverges from if)
existing_state: AssertCommand textually substitutes variables into the condition string and then parses the result as an expression (`context.SubstituteVariables(step.Assert.Condition)` then `evaluator.Evaluate(condition)`, Services/Scripting/Commands/AssertCommand.cs:18-24), whereas IfCommand passes the raw condition to the same ExpressionEvaluator, which resolves variable references internally (IfCommand.cs:24-28). Consequence: for `assert: '"{{output}}" contains "up"'`, any double quote, backslash, or operator-looking text in the device output is spliced into the expression source — typically producing 'Assert condition evaluation failed' (caught at 26-31, fails the step) on data that the logically identical `if:` handles fine; in unlucky cases the spliced text parses as a different expression and the assertion evaluates the wrong thing. Real device output (banners, JSON, quoted strings) hits this routinely, and the same condition string behaves differently between if and assert.
recommendation: Have AssertCommand pass step.Assert.Condition raw to ExpressionEvaluator exactly like IfCommand (delete the SubstituteVariables call at line 18; keep substitution for the `message` only). If some existing scripts rely on {{var}} splicing inside assert conditions, support both: try raw evaluation first and only fall back to substituted text when the raw parse references no resolvable form — but converging on the if semantics is the clean fix.
user_benefit: Assertions stop failing spuriously (or evaluating the wrong predicate) whenever device output contains quotes or operator characters, and if/assert finally agree on what the same condition string means.

evidence.note: substitute-then-parse; parse exception fails the step
if passes the raw condition; evaluator resolves variables itself

title: input validate regex runs with no timeout on the UI thread — a pathological pattern freezes the whole app
existing_state: InputCommand compiles the user-supplied `validate:` pattern with `new Regex(step.Input.Validate, RegexOptions.Compiled)` and no match timeout (Services/Scripting/Commands/InputCommand.cs:41). The match executes in the dialog's OK handler on the UI thread (`_validationRegex.IsMatch(_txtInput.Text)` in BtnOk_Click, InputCommand.cs:209). A backtracking-prone pattern (e.g. `^(\w+\s?)*$`) combined with a longish non-matching input hangs the entire WinForms message pump indefinitely — no Stop button, no recovery except killing the process. The codebase already has the fix pattern: ScriptRegexDefaults.UserPatternTimeout (5s, Services/Scripting/ScriptRegexDefaults.cs:10) is used for the same class of user-authored patterns in ExtractCommand.cs:60 and ExpressionEvaluator.cs:98 — input validation is the one place it was missed.
recommendation: Pass ScriptRegexDefaults.UserPatternTimeout as the third Regex constructor argument at InputCommand.cs:41, and catch RegexMatchTimeoutException in BtnOk_Click (treat as validation failure with a 'pattern timed out' message). Optionally drop RegexOptions.Compiled, which buys nothing for a few interactive matches.
user_benefit: A typo'd validation regex in a script can no longer hard-freeze the app mid-fleet-run at an interactive prompt, taking the unsent work of the whole run with it.

evidence.note: Regex compiled without timeout
IsMatch on the UI thread in BtnOk_Click
5s UserPatternTimeout exists and is used by extract and the expression evaluator

title: Retry loop mutates the shared step.OnError field; concurrent parallel/subroutine reuse of a step races
existing_state: The retry path temporarily rewrites the step object's OnError and restores it in a finally: `var originalOnError = step.OnError; ... step.OnError = onErrorForAttempt; try { ... } finally { step.OnError = originalOnError; }` (ScriptExecutor.cs:456-471). ScriptStep instances are not per-execution copies — subroutine bodies are parsed once and the same `ScriptSubroutineDefinition.Subroutine.Steps` instances are executed every call. ParallelCommand runs each branch on the shared context concurrently via Task.Run (ParallelCommand.cs:40-61) with the comment 'Steps share one context'. So if two parallel branches both `call:` the same subroutine (or a parallel branch and the main flow re-enter the same shared step) and that step has `retry:`, the two executions write/restore the same `step.OnError` without synchronization — one branch can permanently observe the other's forced 'stop', or have its original on_error wiped to the interleaved value, changing whether failures are suppressed. The same shared-instance hazard touches `step.StepPath ??=` (ScriptExecutor.cs:318), though that one is idempotent.
recommendation: Stop mutating shared step state for retry: thread the per-attempt on_error override as a parameter into ExecuteStepCoreAsync / the command result evaluation instead of writing step.OnError, so retry attempts never touch the shared ScriptStep. This also makes retries safe under Parallel and concurrent subroutine calls.
user_benefit: Retries inside parallel blocks or shared subroutines behave deterministically instead of intermittently flipping error-handling behavior under concurrency.

evidence.note: retry mutates and restores shared step.OnError
branches run concurrently on the shared context/steps

title: Capture-mode 'natural completion' can fire early on prompt-like output, killing the still-running remote command
existing_state: Capture mode (interactive with `command:`) decides the command is finished per received chunk: after dispatch, `ShouldArmCaptureNaturalCompletion` arms on the first chunk that contains the command text as a case-insensitive substring of any line (Services/Terminal/InteractiveTerminalService.cs:2690-2712) OR simply isn't prompt-terminated (2674-2683) — i.e., effectively any output arms it. Completion then triggers when the last non-empty line of a chunk matches the detected prompt regex, falling back to `PromptDetector.IsLikelyPrompt` heuristics when startup prompt detection failed (2714-2734; call sites 800-814 windowed, 1390-1404 headless). Chunk boundaries are arbitrary network reads, so a mid-output chunk ending on a prompt-looking line (device status dumps echoing `hostname #`, log lines ending in `$`/`>`, cat of a session log) completes the capture early. On `natural_complete` the step returns Ok with the truncated transcript (563) and the `finally` block disconnects the separate SSH session (573-575) — terminating the still-running remote command (the canonical use case is long-running operations like upgrades), while the step and any `capture:` variable report success.
recommendation: Make completion stricter: require the prompt match to be anchored at the true end of accumulated output (carry an incomplete-final-line buffer like the transcript path already does, rather than testing each raw chunk), require the detected prompt regex when available instead of `IsLikelyPrompt`, and debounce — confirm the prompt persists across a short quiet window (e.g. 300-500 ms with no further output) before declaring `natural_complete`. Keep `max_seconds`/`max_lines` as the hard caps.
user_benefit: Prevents the worst capture failure mode: a long-running command (firmware upgrade, migration) being SIGHUP-killed mid-flight because its own output happened to look like a prompt, while the script reports the step as successfully completed with a truncated transcript.

evidence.note: arming returns true for any non-prompt chunk or any line containing the command substring
case-insensitive substring echo match; completion tests only the last line of the current chunk; IsLikelyPrompt fallback
per-chunk arm/complete in both windowed and headless capture loops
